To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the 16,000-dalton light chain of myosin from Physarum polycephalum inhibits actin polymerization in a calcium-dependent manner.
the actin-modulating activity of CaLc is dependent on the Ca2+ concentration.
CaLc inhibits the actin-actin interactions under high shearing conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of the actomyosin system by CaLc.
the Ca2+-dependent interaction between Physarum myofilaments, which is mediated by CaLc, and the actin-modulating activity of CaLc.
the regulation of actin filament assembly by Physarum CaLc, which is a Ca-binding protein of the 10-kDa class.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CaLc is an actin modulating protein which can be used to study actin filament dynamics in vitro.
the CaLc of Physarum binds to actin in a calcium-dependent manner and that the actin-modulating activity of CaLc is due to its ability to inhibit the polymerization of actin.
actin polymerization is not inhibited by CaLc and that actin is fragmented by CaLc in the presence of a high concentration of Ca2+.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CaLc is a Ca2+-binding protein that modulates actin polymerization in a Ca2+ concentration-dependent manner.
the CaLc-actin interaction is a Ca-dependent inhibitory mechanism for actin filament polymerization.
CaLc inhibits the actin-myosin interaction by reducing the affinity between the myosin heads and the actin filament.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CaLc can act as a regulator of actin polymerization, but the mechanism of regulation is different from the regulation of actin polymerizaton by skeletal muscle myosin light chains.
the CaLc-actin interaction is not a simple on/off process but is dependent on shear forces.
Ca2+ and CaLc are involved in a mechanism for the regulation of the actin filament network in the slime mold Physarum.
